learn.title: Cloud computing fundamentals
objectives: Define cloud computing and recognise what makes a service 'cloud' rather than traditional hosting.
Name the main categories of cloud resources: compute, storage, networking, databases, identity and software.
Explain the consumption-based model and how it differs from buying hardware.
Recognise the three cloud models (public, private, hybrid) and the three service types (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) at an introductory level.
Describe what serverless means and what it does not mean.
Use correct current Azure terminology (for example, Microsoft Entra ID rather than Azure Active Directory).
concepts: Cloud computing

The delivery of computing services (servers, storage, databases, networking, software, analytics and more) over the internet, with on-demand access and payment based on what you use. The provider owns and runs the physical datacenters; you rent capacity.
On-demand self-service
You create resources yourself through a portal, command line or API, usually in minutes, without raising a purchase order or waiting for someone to rack a server.
Broad network access
Services are reachable over the network from many kinds of device: browsers, phones, scripts and other services.
Resource pooling and multitenancy
The provider's physical hardware is shared by many customers. Each customer's resources are logically isolated from the others.
Rapid elasticity
Capacity can grow and shrink quickly, sometimes automatically, to match demand.
Measured service
Usage is metered (for example, compute hours or gigabytes stored), which makes pay-per-use billing possible.
Virtualization
A hypervisor lets one physical server run many isolated virtual machines. Cloud providers build on it to share hardware efficiently.
Consumption-based model
No upfront hardware cost. You pay for what you use, add resources when you need them, and stop paying when you remove them. Spending becomes an operational expense (OpEx).
Economies of scale
Large providers buy hardware, power and network capacity in huge volumes, which lowers the cost per unit and lets them charge less than a small datacenter would cost to run.
Serverless

Servers still exist, but the provider manages them completely. You deploy code or logic, it runs in response to events, it scales automatically, and you are billed for executions or the resources used while it runs. Example: Azure Functions.
terms: An application or group of resources that delivers one business capability.
Allocating and configuring a resource so it is ready to use.
A geographic area containing one or more Azure datacenters connected by a low-latency network.
A physically separate group of datacenters inside a region, with independent power, cooling and networking.
The delay between a request and its response. Distance between users and the region is a major factor.
Moving existing virtual machines to the cloud largely unchanged, usually onto IaaS.
Microsoft's cloud identity service. Its former name, Azure Active Directory (Azure AD), is outdated.
Free amounts of popular services for 12 months, a credit to spend in the first 30 days, and some services that are always free.
services: Azure Virtual Machines
Compute (IaaS): full control of the operating system.
Azure App Service
Compute (PaaS): host web apps and APIs without managing servers.
Azure Functions
Compute (serverless): run code in response to events.
Azure Blob Storage
Storage: object storage for unstructured data such as images, video and backups.
Azure Virtual Network
Networking: a private network for your Azure resources.
Azure SQL Database
Database (PaaS): managed relational database; Microsoft handles patching and backups.
Microsoft Entra ID
Identity: users, groups, sign-in and single sign-on.
Microsoft 365
SaaS: ready-to-use productivity software delivered from the cloud.
Azure Arc
Extends Azure management to servers and Kubernetes clusters running on-premises or in other clouds.
Azure VMware Solution
Runs VMware workloads on dedicated hosts in Azure.
examples: A retailer adds web servers for a holiday sale and removes them in January, paying only for the weeks they ran.
A photo app triggers an Azure Function whenever a user uploads an image, to create a thumbnail. Nothing runs, and almost nothing is billed, between uploads.
A startup launches in a European and an Asian Azure region on the same afternoon without building a datacenter.
A bank keeps a regulated core system on-premises and runs its customer website in Azure: a hybrid cloud.
comparisons: Cloud: self-service, minutes to provision, metered pay-per-use, shared pooled hardware. Traditional hosting or colocation: fixed contracts, manual setup, often your own hardware.
CapEx is upfront spending on physical assets (buying servers). OpEx is spending on services as you consume them (cloud bills).
IaaS: you manage the OS and up. PaaS: you manage the app and data; the platform handles the OS. SaaS: you just use the software and manage your data and users.
Public: provider-owned, shared by many customers. Private: used by one organisation. Hybrid: public and private connected together.
Scale up (vertical): a bigger VM with more CPU or RAM. Scale out (horizontal): more VM instances.
traps: 'Serverless' does not mean there are no servers. It means you don't manage them.
Moving to the cloud never removes all of your security responsibility. Your data, accounts and devices are always yours to protect.
Cloud does not guarantee lower costs. Oversized or forgotten resources keep billing.
A region is not the same thing as an availability zone. Zones are inside a region.
Customers cannot visit Azure datacenters or pick the exact physical server they run on.
Azure Active Directory is now Microsoft Entra ID. Expect the new name on the exam.
revision: Cloud = computing services over the internet, self-service, metered, on shared provider hardware.
Consumption model = no upfront cost, pay for what you use, stop paying when you stop using.
Provider always owns: physical datacenter, physical network, physical hosts.
Customer always owns: data, devices, accounts and identities.
Serverless = event-driven, auto-scaling, pay per execution, no server management.
Reservations suit steady 24/7 workloads; Spot VMs suit interruptible batch work.
Choose a region near your users for lower latency, and in the right geography for data residency.

questions.q: Which statement best defines cloud computing?
opts: Storing backup tapes in an offsite vault managed by a courier company
Connecting the computers in one office building with a local area network
The delivery of computing services such as servers, storage, databases, networking and software over the internet, paid for based on use
Running every business application locally on employees' laptops
questions.e: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of IT resources over the internet. A provider such as Microsoft owns and runs the datacenters; you rent compute, storage, networking, databases and software and typically pay only for what you use. The key ideas are remote delivery over a network, self-service access, and usage-based payment.
why: Offsite tape storage is a traditional backup practice. There is no on-demand computing service and no internet delivery.
A LAN connects local devices. It is networking inside one site, not consumption of services from a provider.
Local laptop software is the opposite of cloud: nothing is delivered from a provider's datacenter.
questions.tip: Look for three clues together: 'over the internet', 'services', and 'pay for what you use'.

questions.q: In a public cloud such as Azure, who owns and maintains the physical servers that run customer workloads?
opts: The cloud provider
The customer's internet service provider
Each customer, for the servers its workloads run on
A hardware reseller chosen by each customer
questions.e: In a public cloud the provider (Microsoft, for Azure) buys, installs, powers, cools, repairs and eventually replaces the physical hardware. Customers rent capacity on that hardware. This is why cloud customers avoid upfront hardware spending and hardware maintenance work.
why: An ISP only provides internet connectivity. It has no role in running the provider's servers.
Customers don't own the hardware in a public cloud. If they did, it would be on-premises or colocation, not public cloud.
Customers don't choose or manage resellers for Azure hardware; Microsoft runs its own supply chain.
questions.tip: Public cloud = provider-owned hardware. 'Physical' anything is the provider's job.

questions.q: A developer at a startup signs in to the Azure portal and creates a new virtual machine in a few minutes, without contacting anyone at Microsoft or waiting for hardware. Which cloud characteristic does this demonstrate?
opts: Fault tolerance
On-demand self-service
Resource pooling
Broad network access
questions.e: On-demand self-service means customers can provision resources themselves, whenever they want, through a portal, CLI or API, with no human interaction on the provider side. It replaces the traditional cycle of purchase orders, delivery and racking servers, which could take weeks.
why: Fault tolerance is the ability to keep running when a component fails. Nothing in the scenario involves a failure.
Resource pooling describes the provider sharing hardware among many customers. The scenario is about the developer acting alone and instantly.
Broad network access is about reaching services from many devices and locations, not about creating resources without help.
questions.tip: 'Without contacting anyone' and 'in minutes' point to self-service.

questions.q: A cloud provider runs workloads for thousands of companies on the same physical servers, while keeping each company's resources logically isolated. What is this arrangement called?
opts: Multitenancy
Hybrid cloud
Vertical scaling
Private cloud
questions.e: Multitenancy means many customers (tenants) share the same underlying physical infrastructure, with software-enforced isolation between them. It is how public cloud providers pool resources efficiently and achieve economies of scale. Your data and resources stay separate even though the hardware is shared.
why: Hybrid cloud combines public and private environments. It says nothing about many customers sharing hardware.
Vertical scaling means giving one resource more CPU or memory. It is unrelated to sharing infrastructure.
A private cloud is dedicated to a single organisation, which is the opposite of many tenants sharing hardware.
questions.tip: 'Many customers, same hardware, isolated' = multitenancy (resource pooling).

questions.q: Azure records how many hours a virtual machine runs and how many gigabytes are stored, then bills the customer for that usage. Which cloud characteristic makes this possible?
opts: Capital expenditure
Multitenancy
Broad network access
Measured service
questions.e: Measured service means the provider meters resource usage (compute time, storage, data transfer, transactions) automatically. Metering is what makes the consumption-based, pay-as-you-go model work: your bill reflects what you actually consumed.
why: Capital expenditure is upfront spending on physical assets, which is the opposite of metered usage billing.
Multitenancy explains how hardware is shared. It doesn't describe how usage is measured.
Broad network access is about reaching services from many devices, not about tracking and billing usage.
questions.tip: Billing based on metered usage = measured service.

questions.q: Sales staff use a cloud-hosted CRM application from office PCs, home laptops and smartphones while travelling. Which cloud characteristic does this illustrate?
opts: Economies of scale
Rapid elasticity
Broad network access
On-demand self-service
questions.e: Broad network access means cloud services are available over the network through standard mechanisms, so many kinds of client (browsers, mobile apps, scripts) can reach them from anywhere with connectivity. It is one reason cloud supports remote and mobile work so well.
why: Economies of scale explain why providers can price services lower. They don't describe device access.
Rapid elasticity is about capacity growing and shrinking with demand. The scenario is about where and how users connect.
On-demand self-service is about provisioning resources without provider interaction, not about which devices can use an app.
questions.tip: Many device types, many locations = broad network access.

questions.q: Which category of cloud service does an Azure virtual machine belong to?
opts: Identity
Networking
Storage
Compute
questions.e: Compute services provide processing power to run applications and code. Azure Virtual Machines are the classic compute service: they supply virtual CPU and memory to run an operating system and your software. Other compute options include App Service, containers and Azure Functions.
why: Identity services, such as Microsoft Entra ID, manage users and sign-in. They don't run workloads.
A VM connects to a virtual network, but networking services are things like Azure Virtual Network and VPN Gateway.
A VM uses disks, but the VM itself is a compute resource. Storage services include Blob Storage and Azure Files.
questions.tip: If it runs code or an operating system, it's compute.

questions.q: Which technology allows a cloud provider to run many isolated virtual machines on a single physical server?
opts: A hypervisor (virtualization)
A content delivery network
The Domain Name System (DNS)
A load balancer
questions.e: A hypervisor abstracts the physical hardware so that multiple virtual machines, each with its own operating system, can run side by side in isolation on one host. Virtualization is a foundation of cloud computing because it lets providers pool and share hardware efficiently.
why: A CDN caches content close to users to speed delivery. It doesn't create VMs.
DNS translates domain names to IP addresses. It doesn't divide servers into virtual machines.
A load balancer spreads traffic across servers. It doesn't create virtual machines on a host.
questions.tip: 'Many VMs on one physical server' = hypervisor.

questions.q: Under the cloud consumption-based model, what does a customer pay for?
opts: A fixed amount based on the maximum capacity it might ever need
A one-time licence fee that covers unlimited future use
The purchase price of the servers allocated to it
The resources it actually uses, when it uses them
questions.e: The consumption-based model means no upfront hardware costs: you pay for what you use, add resources when you need them, and stop paying for resources you remove. It turns IT spending into an operational expense that tracks actual demand.
why: Paying for peak capacity up front is the on-premises pattern the cloud avoids.
A single licence fee for unlimited use isn't how cloud consumption billing works; usage is metered continuously.
Customers never buy the provider's servers. They rent capacity.
questions.tip: 'Pay for what you use' is the definition. Anything fixed or upfront is a distractor.

questions.q: An online retailer's traffic triples during a two-week holiday sale each year. With on-premises servers it had to buy hardware for the peak, which sat idle the rest of the year. How does the cloud change this?
opts: The retailer can add capacity for the sale and remove it afterwards, paying only while the extra resources run
The retailer must sign a yearly contract sized for the peak traffic
The retailer must still buy capacity for the peak, but the cloud provider stores the servers
The provider absorbs the peak at no cost because cloud capacity is unlimited and free
questions.e: The cloud lets you match capacity to demand. The retailer scales out for the sale and scales back in afterwards. Because billing is consumption-based, it stops paying for the extra capacity once it's removed, instead of owning idle hardware all year.
why: Pay-as-you-go doesn't require a yearly contract sized for peak. Commitments such as reservations are optional and suit steady workloads.
Buying for the peak is exactly the on-premises problem. Cloud customers don't purchase servers.
Extra capacity is billed. It isn't free, and you still pay for what you consume.
questions.tip: Temporary spikes plus 'pay only while running' point to scalability under the consumption model.

questions.q: Is the following statement true or false? 'After a company moves its workloads to Azure, Microsoft is responsible for all aspects of the company's security.'
opts: False. The customer becomes responsible for the physical security of Azure datacenters
False. The customer always remains responsible for its data, devices, accounts and identities
True, but only for workloads that use SaaS services
True. Moving to the cloud transfers all security responsibility to the provider
questions.e: Under the shared responsibility model, Microsoft secures the physical infrastructure (datacenters, physical network and hosts). Whatever the service type, the customer always keeps responsibility for its information and data, the devices that connect, and its accounts and identities. Other areas move between customer and provider depending on IaaS, PaaS or SaaS.
why: Physical datacenter security is always Microsoft's responsibility, never the customer's.
Even in SaaS the customer still owns its data, user accounts and devices.
Security is never fully transferred. Data and identities remain the customer's responsibility.
questions.tip: Watch for absolute words like 'all'. In shared responsibility, data, devices and identities always stay with you.

questions.q: A small software company spends much of its IT budget and staff time replacing failed disks, patching hypervisors and upgrading datacenter cooling. What is the main benefit it gains by moving to the cloud?
opts: Staff can spend more time on building and running the company's applications instead of maintaining physical infrastructure
Its applications will automatically be rewritten as cloud-native services
The company gains direct physical access to the provider's datacenters
The company no longer needs to secure its applications or user accounts
questions.e: Moving to the cloud shifts physical infrastructure work, such as hardware repair, power, cooling and host maintenance, to the provider. The company's staff can then focus on what differentiates the business: its applications, data and customers.
why: Moving to the cloud doesn't rewrite applications. Modernising them is separate work the customer chooses to do.
Customers have no physical access to Azure datacenters. Microsoft tightly restricts it.
Application and account security remain the customer's responsibility in every service type.
questions.tip: 'Stop maintaining hardware, focus on the business' is a core cloud value statement.

questions.q: What is Microsoft Azure?
opts: A private datacenter appliance that companies buy and install on-premises
A programming language for building web applications
A public cloud computing platform that offers a broad range of services, operated by Microsoft in datacenters worldwide
An operating system installed on each employee's PC
questions.e: Azure is Microsoft's public cloud platform. It offers hundreds of services (compute, storage, networking, databases, AI, identity, management tools) delivered from Microsoft-operated datacenters around the world. Customers sign up, create resources on demand, and pay for what they use.
why: Azure is consumed as a service from Microsoft's datacenters, not bought as an appliance for your own building.
Azure supports many programming languages, but it isn't a language itself.
Windows is an operating system. Azure is a cloud platform you reach over the network.
questions.tip: Azure = Microsoft's public cloud platform.

questions.q: Which statement about Azure datacenters is correct?
opts: Every Azure customer is given its own dedicated datacenter building
All Azure services run from a single global datacenter
Customers can choose the specific rack and server where their virtual machine runs
Microsoft operates datacenters around the world and groups them into regions that customers choose from
questions.e: Azure datacenters are facilities full of racks, with their own power, cooling and networking. Customers don't pick individual datacenters or servers. Instead they choose a region, a geographic area containing one or more datacenters, and Azure places resources within it.
why: Datacenters are shared by many customers (multitenancy). They aren't dedicated buildings.
Azure has many datacenters across many regions worldwide, not one.
Customers choose a region (and optionally an availability zone), never a rack or a physical host.
questions.tip: You pick a region, not a building or a server.

questions.q:
Evaluate these statements about cloud computing.
1. Cloud resources can be created through a web portal, a command-line tool or an API.
2. Using cloud services always requires a long-term contract with a minimum spend.
3. Large cloud providers can offer lower unit prices partly because of economies of scale.
Which statements are true?
opts: Statements 1, 2 and 3
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
questions.e: Statement 1 is true: Azure resources can be managed through the Azure portal, Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell and REST APIs. Statement 3 is true: buying hardware, power and bandwidth at huge volume lowers cost per unit. Statement 2 is false: pay-as-you-go needs no long-term commitment. Commitments such as reservations are optional discounts.
why: Statement 2 is false, so 'all three' can't be right.
Statement 2 is false, and this choice also leaves out true statement 1.
Statement 2 is false. Pay-as-you-go has no long-term contract requirement.
questions.tip: In multi-statement questions, judge each statement on its own first. The word 'always' is often the giveaway.

questions.q: Why can a large public cloud provider often offer compute at a lower unit cost than a small company could achieve in its own datacenter?
opts: It buys hardware, power and network capacity at enormous volume, which lowers the cost per unit
It's exempt from paying for electricity in most countries
It doesn't need to staff its datacenters
It runs each customer on dedicated hardware that never needs replacing
questions.e: Economies of scale mean that doing something at very large scale lowers the cost per unit. Cloud providers buy servers, energy and bandwidth in vast quantities and run them very efficiently, and part of that saving is passed on to customers through lower prices.
why: Providers pay for electricity like anyone else. Power is one of their largest costs.
Datacenters still need skilled staff. Scale makes staffing more efficient but doesn't remove it.
Cloud hardware is shared (multitenant) and is replaced regularly. Neither claim is true.
questions.tip: 'Lower cost because the provider is huge' = economies of scale.

questions.q: A company wants a small piece of code to run only when a file is uploaded, scale automatically with the number of uploads, and cost nothing to keep a server running between uploads. Which approach fits best?
opts: A virtual machine that runs continuously
A private cloud cluster in the company's datacenter
Serverless computing
A dedicated physical server leased for three years
questions.e: Serverless computing (for example, Azure Functions) runs code in response to events such as a file upload. The provider manages the servers, scales instances automatically, and on consumption plans bills for executions and the resources they use, so idle time costs little or nothing.
why: A continuously running VM is billed while it runs, even when idle, and you manage its operating system.
A private cloud requires the company to own and run the infrastructure, which is the opposite of the requirement.
A leased physical server is a fixed cost whether or not uploads occur.
questions.tip: 'Run when an event happens' plus 'no idle cost' = serverless.

questions.q: Which statement about serverless computing is accurate?
opts: Serverless code runs directly on users' devices, so no servers are involved
Servers still exist, but the cloud provider provisions, scales and maintains them, so you don't manage any servers
Serverless means the application has no back end and stores no data
Serverless requires you to patch the underlying operating system yourself
questions.e: 'Serverless' is about who manages the servers, not whether they exist. The provider handles provisioning, scaling, patching and availability of the infrastructure. You focus on code or workflow logic, which runs on demand and is billed by consumption.
why: Serverless code runs in the provider's datacenters, not on end-user devices.
Serverless apps can have rich back ends and can store data in databases and storage services.
Patching the operating system is exactly the work serverless removes from you.
questions.tip: Trap: 'serverless' does not mean 'no servers'. It means no servers for you to manage.

questions.on: Identify appropriate use cases for each cloud service type
questions.q: Which of the following is an example of software as a service (SaaS)?
opts: Azure App Service
Azure Virtual Machines
Azure Virtual Network
Microsoft 365
questions.e: SaaS delivers complete, ready-to-use applications. The provider runs everything (infrastructure, platform and the application itself), and users simply sign in and use the software. Microsoft 365 (email, Office apps, Teams) is a classic SaaS example.
why: Azure App Service is PaaS: you deploy your own code onto a managed platform.
Azure Virtual Machines are IaaS: you manage the operating system and everything installed on it.
Azure Virtual Network is a networking building block used with IaaS and PaaS. It isn't a finished application.
questions.tip: If end users just sign in and use a finished app, it's SaaS.

questions.on: Identify appropriate use cases for each cloud service type
questions.q: A company must run a legacy application that needs a specific operating system version and custom drivers installed on the server. It wants to stop buying hardware. Which cloud service type fits best?
opts: Infrastructure as a service (IaaS)
Platform as a service (PaaS)
Serverless functions
Software as a service (SaaS)
questions.e: IaaS gives you virtual machines, storage and networking while the provider manages the physical hardware. You keep full control of the operating system, so you can install specific OS versions, drivers and software. That makes it the usual home for legacy applications that need server-level customisation.
why: PaaS manages the operating system for you, so you can't install custom drivers or pin an OS version.
Serverless runs event-driven code on infrastructure you don't control, which is unsuitable for apps that need OS customisation.
SaaS offers finished applications. You can't install your own legacy app or drivers.
questions.tip: 'Full control of the OS' or 'custom drivers' = IaaS.

questions.on: Identify appropriate use cases for each cloud service type
questions.q: A development team wants to deploy a web application's code without having to patch operating systems or manage the underlying servers, while keeping control of the application itself. Which service type fits best?
opts: Software as a service (SaaS)
Platform as a service (PaaS)
Infrastructure as a service (IaaS)
On-premises virtualization
questions.e: PaaS provides a managed platform (runtime, operating system, middleware and infrastructure) onto which you deploy your own code. The provider handles OS patching and server management, and you manage the application and its data. Azure App Service is a common PaaS example.
why: SaaS provides someone else's finished application. The team needs to run its own code.
IaaS would leave the team patching and managing the operating system, which it wants to avoid.
On-premises virtualization keeps all the server and hardware management with the company.
questions.tip: 'Deploy my code, don't manage the OS' = PaaS.

questions.q: What does an organisation need before it can create resources such as virtual machines in Azure?
opts: An Azure account with an Azure subscription
A dedicated network circuit to a Microsoft datacenter
A physical server to host the virtual machine
An on-premises hypervisor cluster
questions.e: To use Azure you need an account, which gives you access to one or more subscriptions. A subscription is the billing and management boundary that resources are created in. No hardware or special network connection is needed. Internet access to the portal or APIs is enough to start.
why: A dedicated circuit (such as ExpressRoute) is optional. Resources can be created and reached over the internet.
Azure provides the physical servers. You don't supply hardware.
Azure runs its own hypervisors. You don't need on-premises virtualization.
questions.tip: Account, then subscription, then resources.

questions.q: Which scenario best represents cloud computing rather than traditional hosting?
opts: Renting rack space in a facility and shipping your own servers there
Creating virtual machines through a self-service portal in minutes and being billed for the time they run
Buying servers and installing them in a room in your own office
Leasing a dedicated physical server on a fixed three-year contract that the host sets up manually
questions.e: Cloud computing combines on-demand self-service, rapid provisioning and metered, usage-based billing on provider-owned, pooled infrastructure. Creating VMs yourself in minutes and paying for runtime shows all three.
why: Renting rack space for your own servers is colocation: you still buy and maintain the hardware.
Buying servers for your own office is on-premises infrastructure, a capital expense.
A fixed-term manually provisioned server lacks self-service and usage-based billing.
questions.tip: Self-service, minutes and metered billing together mean cloud. Fixed contracts and your own hardware mean traditional.

questions.q: A company replaces its server hardware every five years, which needs large capital budgets and months of migration work. After moving its workloads to Azure IaaS virtual machines, who handles replacing the underlying physical servers?
opts: No one, because cloud hardware never needs to be replaced
The company, which must schedule and pay for hardware refreshes in Azure
The company's managed service provider, which must ship new servers to Microsoft
Microsoft, as part of operating the Azure datacenters
questions.e: Physical infrastructure, including servers, storage hardware, network devices and their lifecycle, is always the provider's responsibility. Microsoft replaces aging or failed hardware behind the scenes. Customers rent virtual capacity, so the hardware refresh cycle and its capital cost disappear from their planning.
why: Cloud hardware does wear out and is replaced. The difference is that the provider does it.
In Azure the customer never buys or refreshes physical servers, even with IaaS.
Partners don't supply hardware to Azure datacenters; Microsoft manages its own hardware.
questions.tip: Even in IaaS, everything physical belongs to the provider.

questions.q: A company needs a place in the cloud to keep millions of images, videos and backup files. Which category of cloud service does it need?
opts: Networking
Storage
Compute
Identity
questions.e: Storage services hold data persistently. Azure Storage includes Blob Storage, which is optimised for large amounts of unstructured data such as images, video and backups, along with Azure Files, Queue Storage and Table Storage.
why: Networking services connect resources. They don't store files.
Compute services process data and run code. They aren't built to hold millions of files.
Identity services manage who can sign in and what they can access, not file data.
questions.tip: Keeping files or objects means storage. Running code means compute.

questions.on: Define cloud models, including public, private, and hybrid
questions.q: Which description matches a public cloud?
opts: Infrastructure used exclusively by one organisation and managed by its own IT team
A laptop running a local virtual machine for testing
Infrastructure owned and operated by a cloud provider, with services available to many organisations over the internet
A single company's servers connected to a partner's servers through a private link
questions.e: A public cloud is built, owned and maintained by a third-party provider such as Microsoft. Anyone who wants to buy services can use it, and customers share the underlying infrastructure while staying logically isolated. Benefits include no capital expenditure, rapid provisioning, and pay-as-you-go pricing.
why: Exclusive use by one organisation describes a private cloud.
A local test VM on a laptop is desktop virtualization, not cloud computing.
Two companies' servers joined by a private link is just a network connection, not a public cloud.
questions.tip: Public = provider-owned and available to anyone who pays.

questions.on: Define cloud models, including public, private, and hybrid
questions.q: Which statement about a private cloud is correct?
opts: Its cloud resources are used by a single organisation, and it can be hosted in that organisation's own datacenter or by a third party
It cannot use virtualization or self-service provisioning
Many unrelated organisations share it, as in a public cloud
It is always cheaper than a public cloud because there is no provider markup
questions.e: A private cloud provides cloud-style capabilities (virtualization, self-service, automation) for one organisation only. It offers maximum control over hardware and security, but the organisation bears the cost and responsibility of buying, maintaining and upgrading the infrastructure.
why: Private clouds do use virtualization and self-service. That's what makes them clouds and not just a server room.
Sharing among unrelated organisations describes a public cloud.
Private clouds usually need significant capital spending and staff, so they're often more expensive, not less.
questions.tip: Private = one organisation, maximum control, you pay for the hardware.

questions.on: Identify appropriate use cases for each cloud model
questions.q: A hospital must keep a patient-records database in its own datacenter for regulatory reasons, but wants to host its public appointment-booking website in Azure. The website reads availability data from the on-premises database. Which cloud model is this?
opts: Private cloud
Public cloud
Hybrid cloud
Software as a service
questions.e: A hybrid cloud combines a public cloud with private (on-premises) infrastructure and lets data and applications interact across them. It suits organisations that need to keep some workloads on-premises for compliance or latency reasons while using public cloud scale and agility for others.
why: A purely private cloud would keep the website on-premises too, which isn't what's happening.
A purely public cloud would mean the database also lives in Azure, which the hospital can't do.
SaaS is a service type, not a deployment model, and the hospital runs its own website.
questions.tip: Part on-premises plus part public cloud, connected together = hybrid.

questions.on: Define cloud models, including public, private, and hybrid
questions.q: A company runs its data analytics in Azure and its e-commerce platform on another public cloud provider. It has no on-premises datacenter. Which term best describes this environment?
opts: Hybrid cloud
Multicloud
Single-tenant cloud
Private cloud
questions.e: Multicloud means using two or more public cloud providers, often to take advantage of different features or to avoid depending on one vendor. Managing several environments adds complexity, and tools such as Azure Arc can help bring them under one management approach.
why: Hybrid cloud combines public cloud with private infrastructure. This company has no on-premises or private cloud.
'Single-tenant' describes dedicated hardware, not using several providers.
A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation and owned or hosted for it. These are public clouds.
questions.tip: Several public providers = multicloud. Public plus private = hybrid.

questions.on: Describe the purpose of Azure Arc
questions.q: A company has Windows and Linux servers in its own datacenter and Kubernetes clusters on another cloud provider. It wants to view, govern and apply Azure Policy to all of them from Azure, without migrating them. Which Azure service should it use?
opts: Azure Data Box
Azure VMware Solution
Azure Arc
Azure Migrate
questions.e: Azure Arc extends Azure's management and governance to resources outside Azure: servers, Kubernetes clusters and some data services running on-premises or in other clouds. Once connected, they appear in Azure Resource Manager and can be organised, tagged, monitored and governed with Azure Policy alongside native Azure resources.
why: Azure Data Box is a physical device for transferring large amounts of data into Azure.
Azure VMware Solution runs VMware workloads inside Azure. It doesn't manage servers that stay where they are.
Azure Migrate assesses and moves workloads into Azure, but the company doesn't want to migrate.
questions.tip: 'Manage from Azure without moving it', for on-premises or multicloud resources = Azure Arc.

questions.on: Identify appropriate use cases for each cloud model
questions.q: An organisation runs hundreds of workloads on VMware in its datacenter. It wants to move them to Azure quickly while keeping the same VMware tools and skills. Which option fits best?
opts: Azure VMware Solution
Azure Arc
Azure Functions
Azure Virtual Desktop
questions.e: Azure VMware Solution provides private VMware environments running on dedicated Azure hosts. Organisations can move VMware workloads to Azure with minimal change and keep using familiar VMware tools, then integrate with other Azure services over time.
why: Azure Arc manages resources that stay outside Azure. It doesn't host VMware workloads in Azure.
Azure Functions is serverless code hosting, not a platform for existing VMware VMs.
Azure Virtual Desktop delivers virtual desktops and apps to users. It isn't a VMware migration target.
questions.tip: 'Keep VMware tools, run in Azure' = Azure VMware Solution.

questions.q: A company buys 40 physical servers and the networking equipment for a new on-premises datacenter. What type of spending is this?
opts: Consumption-based spending
Capital expenditure (CapEx)
Operational expenditure (OpEx)
Pay-as-you-go spending
questions.e: Capital expenditure is a one-time, upfront payment for physical assets such as servers, buildings and network equipment. The value of those assets is spread (depreciated) over their useful life. Traditional datacenters rely heavily on CapEx.
why: Consumption-based spending is an OpEx pattern where you pay per use, not an upfront asset purchase.
OpEx is ongoing spending on services or products as they're used, such as a cloud bill.
Pay-as-you-go is the cloud's consumption billing approach, not a hardware purchase.
questions.tip: Buying physical things up front = CapEx.

questions.q: A company pays a monthly Azure bill that varies with the resources it used that month. What type of spending is this?
opts: Capital expenditure (CapEx)
Fixed asset investment
Depreciation expense
Operational expenditure (OpEx)
questions.e: Operational expenditure is spending on services or products as they are consumed, billed as you go. Cloud computing turns IT infrastructure from a capital investment into an operational expense, which gives flexibility and avoids large upfront purchases.
why: CapEx is an upfront purchase of physical assets, not a usage-based monthly bill.
A fixed asset investment means buying long-lived assets, which the company isn't doing.
Depreciation spreads the cost of an owned asset over time. The company doesn't own Azure's hardware.
questions.tip: A monthly bill that changes with usage = OpEx.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of the cloud consumption-based model?
opts: A guaranteed, identical monthly bill regardless of how much you use
The ability to pay for extra resources only when they're needed
The ability to stop paying for resources that are no longer needed
No upfront infrastructure costs
questions.e: The consumption-based model's benefits are no upfront costs, no need to buy and manage costly infrastructure you might not fully use, paying for more resources when needed, and stopping payment when resources are removed. Because billing follows usage, the bill varies. A fixed identical bill isn't a feature of the model.
why: Paying for extra capacity only when needed is a core benefit.
Stopping payment when you remove resources is a core benefit.
No upfront cost is a core benefit of the consumption model.
questions.tip: In 'NOT a benefit' questions, find the option that contradicts pay-for-what-you-use.

questions.q: A company runs a set of virtual machines 24 hours a day, every day, and expects to keep them for at least three years. It currently pays pay-as-you-go rates. Which pricing approach is most likely to reduce cost without changing the workload?
opts: Switch the VMs to Azure Spot Virtual Machines
Stop the VMs every night
Purchase Azure Reservations for a one- or three-year term
Move the VMs to an on-premises private cloud
questions.e: Azure Reservations give a significant discount over pay-as-you-go in return for committing to a resource type and region for one or three years. They suit steady, predictable workloads that run continuously, which is exactly this case.
why: Spot VMs can be evicted at any time when Azure needs capacity back, which doesn't suit a workload that must run 24/7.
Stopping the VMs at night would change the workload, and the company needs them running all day.
Moving on-premises brings back capital spending and hardware management. It isn't a pricing choice within Azure.
questions.tip: Steady and long-running = reservations. Interruptible = Spot. Variable = pay-as-you-go.

questions.q: A research team runs large batch simulations that can be paused and restarted at any time without harm. It wants the lowest possible compute price and accepts that machines may be taken away at short notice. Which option fits best?
opts: Azure Reservations for three years
Azure Spot Virtual Machines
Pay-as-you-go virtual machines
Azure Dedicated Host
questions.e: Azure Spot Virtual Machines use Azure's unused capacity at a deep discount. Azure can evict them with little notice when it needs the capacity back, so they're ideal for interruptible work such as batch jobs, rendering and dev/test.
why: Reservations suit steady workloads that run continuously, not interruptible, irregular batch jobs.
Pay-as-you-go is flexible but costs more than Spot for work that tolerates eviction.
Dedicated Host gives you a whole physical server for isolation or compliance, which raises cost.
questions.tip: 'Can be interrupted' and 'lowest price' = Spot VMs.

questions.q: Which responsibility always belongs to Microsoft, whether a customer uses IaaS, PaaS or SaaS?
opts: Securing the customer's employee devices
Classifying the customer's data
Managing the customer's user accounts
Physical security of the datacenters
questions.e: Under the shared responsibility model, the physical layer (datacenter buildings, physical hosts and the physical network) is always the provider's responsibility. Customers never have physical access to Azure datacenters, so they can't be responsible for securing them.
why: Devices (laptops, phones) that connect to the cloud always stay with the customer.
Data classification and protection always stay with the customer.
Accounts and identities always stay with the customer.
questions.tip: Physical = Microsoft. Data, devices, accounts = you.

questions.q: A company uses only SaaS applications in the cloud. Who is responsible for the accuracy and protection of the information the company stores in those applications?
opts: No one, because SaaS data is automatically protected
The company that owns the data
The internet service provider
The SaaS provider, because it hosts the application
questions.e: Even with SaaS, where the provider runs almost everything, the customer remains responsible for its information and data: what it stores, who it shares it with, how it is classified, and so on. The provider secures the application and infrastructure, but it doesn't own or govern the customer's data.
why: Data is never 'automatically protected' in every respect. Misconfiguration and oversharing are customer risks.
An ISP only provides connectivity and has nothing to do with data inside SaaS apps.
The provider hosts and secures the application, but the data's content and its protection decisions stay with the customer.
questions.tip: Data is always the customer's, in every service type.

questions.q: A company deploys Windows Server on Azure Virtual Machines. Who is responsible for installing security updates on the Windows Server operating system?
opts: The hardware manufacturer
Microsoft, because the VM runs in an Azure datacenter
The customer
Microsoft and the customer must each approve every update
questions.e: In IaaS the provider manages the physical hardware, hosts and network. Everything from the guest operating system upwards (OS patches, installed software, configuration, network controls on the VM) is the customer's responsibility. Azure offers tools such as Azure Update Manager to help, but the responsibility stays with the customer.
why: Hardware manufacturers don't patch guest operating systems.
Microsoft maintains the physical host, not the guest OS inside your IaaS VM.
There's no joint approval process. Guest OS patching in IaaS is solely the customer's job.
questions.tip: IaaS: provider does the physical layer; you do the OS and above.

questions.q: In a SaaS service such as Microsoft 365, who is responsible for maintaining and updating the application code?
opts: The customer's developers
The cloud provider
A third-party auditor
The customer's end users
questions.e: With SaaS the provider manages the application, the platform and the infrastructure. It fixes bugs, adds features and patches the code. The customer manages its data, user accounts, devices and how the application is configured and used.
why: The customer's developers don't have access to SaaS application code.
Auditors assess compliance but don't maintain application code.
End users use the application. They don't maintain its code.
questions.tip: SaaS: the provider runs the app, and you run your data and users.

questions.q:
A company hosts its web app on a PaaS service in Azure. Evaluate these statements.
1. The company must install operating system updates on the servers that run the app.
2. The company is responsible for managing which user accounts can access the app.
3. Microsoft is responsible for the physical network in the datacenter.
Which statements are true?
opts: Statement 3 only
Statements 1, 2 and 3
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
questions.e: In PaaS, Microsoft manages the operating system, runtime and infrastructure, so statement 1 is false. Accounts and identities always stay with the customer, so statement 2 is true. The physical network is always Microsoft's responsibility, so statement 3 is true.
why: This leaves out statement 2, which is true because accounts are always the customer's.
Statement 1 is false, so 'all three' is wrong.
Statement 1 is false. PaaS removes OS patching from the customer.
questions.tip: PaaS shifts OS work to the provider, but identities and data never shift.

questions.on: Describe the benefits of high availability and scalability in the cloud
questions.q: What does high availability mean for a cloud application?
opts: The application can be deployed in many programming languages
The application stays accessible to users for as much of the time as possible, with minimal downtime
The application stores data in more than one format
The application costs the same every month
questions.e: High availability focuses on keeping a service up and reachable despite disruptions. It's often expressed as an uptime percentage in a service-level agreement (SLA), such as 99.9% or 99.99%. Techniques include redundancy across availability zones and load balancing across instances.
why: Language support has nothing to do with uptime.
Storing data in multiple formats doesn't make an application more available.
A predictable monthly cost relates to cost predictability, not availability.
questions.tip: Availability = uptime. Look for 'minimal downtime' or 'accessible'.

questions.on: Describe the benefits of high availability and scalability in the cloud
questions.q: To handle more traffic, an administrator increases the number of web server virtual machines from 3 to 8. What type of scaling is this?
opts: Scaling down
Vertical scaling (scaling up)
Regional failover
Horizontal scaling (scaling out)
questions.e: Horizontal scaling, or scaling out, adds more instances of a resource to share the load, and scaling in removes them. It's well suited to stateless web servers behind a load balancer, and Azure features such as Virtual Machine Scale Sets can do it automatically.
why: Scaling down reduces the size of a resource. Here resources were added.
Vertical scaling makes one machine bigger (more CPU or RAM) rather than adding machines.
Regional failover moves work to another region after an outage. It isn't a way to handle more traffic.
questions.tip: More machines = out (horizontal). Bigger machine = up (vertical).

questions.on: Describe the benefits of high availability and scalability in the cloud
questions.q: A database server running on a single VM is running out of memory. The administrator changes the VM size from 8 GB to 32 GB of RAM. What type of scaling is this?
opts: Vertical scaling (scaling up)
Geo-replication
Horizontal scaling (scaling out)
Scaling in
questions.e: Vertical scaling, or scaling up, increases the capabilities of a single resource, such as more CPU, memory or faster disks, by resizing it. It's useful for workloads that can't easily be split across many machines, such as some databases. Scaling down reduces those capabilities again.
why: Geo-replication copies data to another region for resilience. It doesn't add memory.
Horizontal scaling adds more instances rather than enlarging one.
Scaling in removes instances. Nothing was removed here.
questions.tip: Resize one resource = vertical.

questions.on: Describe the benefits of reliability and predictability in the cloud
questions.q: A company wants its customer-facing application to keep serving users even if an entire Azure region becomes unavailable. Which design choice best supports this goal?
opts: Add more virtual machines in the same availability zone
Deploy the application in at least two Azure regions so that one can take over if the other fails
Increase the size of the virtual machines in the current region
Purchase reservations for the existing virtual machines
questions.e: Reliability is the ability to recover from failures and keep functioning. The cloud's global footprint lets you deploy across regions, so if one region suffers a major outage, another can continue serving users. This is the basis of multi-region disaster recovery designs.
why: More VMs in the same zone still fail together if the region (or that zone) fails.
Bigger VMs improve capacity, not resilience to the loss of a whole region.
Reservations reduce cost. They don't affect resilience.
questions.tip: Surviving a region outage requires a second region.

questions.on: Describe the benefits of reliability and predictability in the cloud
questions.q: In Microsoft's description of cloud benefits, predictability focuses on which two areas?
opts: Performance and cost
Authentication and authorisation
Scalability and elasticity
Regions and availability zones
questions.e: Predictability in the cloud means you can confidently forecast performance (using autoscaling, load balancing and high availability) and cost (using tools such as the pricing calculator and Microsoft Cost Management to track and forecast spending).
why: Authentication and authorisation are identity and security concepts.
Scalability and elasticity are related to performance, but they aren't the two areas of predictability.
Regions and availability zones are architecture components that support reliability.
questions.tip: Predictability = can I predict how it will perform and what it will cost?

questions.on: Describe the benefits of security and governance in the cloud
questions.q: An organisation wants to make sure every resource deployed in the cloud meets company standards, such as being created only in approved regions. Which cloud benefit does this relate to?
opts: Elasticity
Governance
Latency
Agility
questions.e: Governance in the cloud means setting and enforcing rules so that deployments meet corporate and regulatory standards. In Azure this is supported by tools such as Azure Policy and templates, which can audit or prevent non-compliant deployments.
why: Elasticity is about capacity adjusting automatically to demand.
Latency is network delay and has nothing to do with deployment rules.
Agility is about creating and changing resources quickly.
questions.tip: Rules and standards for deployments = governance.

questions.t: Management in vs of the cloud
questions.on: Describe the benefits of manageability in the cloud
questions.q: Microsoft describes manageability as having two parts: management of the cloud and management in the cloud. Which example describes management in the cloud?
opts: Azure monitors resource health and replaces failed resources automatically
Resources scale automatically according to demand
Resources are deployed from a preconfigured template
An administrator uses the Azure portal, Azure CLI or REST APIs to work with resources
questions.e: Management of the cloud means managing the resources themselves: autoscaling, template-based deployment, health monitoring, automatic replacement of failed resources, and alerts. Management in the cloud means how you interact with the environment: through a web portal, a command-line interface, APIs or PowerShell.
why: Health monitoring and automatic replacement are management of the cloud.
Autoscaling is management of the cloud, because it describes what the resources do.
Template-based deployment is management of the cloud.
questions.tip: 'In the cloud' = the tools you use (portal, CLI, API). 'Of the cloud' = what happens to the resources.

questions.on: Describe the benefits of security and governance in the cloud
questions.q: A small company runs its own datacenter with a single internet connection. Why is a large cloud provider generally better placed to withstand a very large distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack?
opts: It has massive global network capacity and dedicated DDoS protection services that can absorb and filter attack traffic
Cloud applications can't be reached from the internet, so they can't be attacked
Cloud providers block all traffic from outside the customer's country
Each cloud customer gets its own private internet backbone
questions.e: DDoS attacks try to overwhelm a service with traffic. A large provider has enormous network capacity and specialised protection (Azure includes infrastructure-level DDoS protection, and Azure DDoS Protection adds tuned mitigation for virtual networks), so it can absorb and filter traffic volumes that would saturate a small company's connection.
why: Cloud applications are often internet-facing by design and can be attacked. The difference is the capacity to absorb attacks.
Providers don't block all foreign traffic; global access is a key cloud benefit.
Customers share the provider's global network. They don't each get a private internet backbone.
questions.tip: Scale is a security benefit: big networks absorb big attacks.

questions.on: Describe the benefits of high availability and scalability in the cloud
questions.q: A development team needs a full test environment for a new feature. Instead of waiting weeks for hardware, it creates the environment in Azure in under an hour and deletes it when testing ends. Which cloud benefit does this best illustrate?
opts: Disaster recovery
Agility
Capital expenditure
Fault tolerance
questions.e: Agility is the ability to create, change and remove resources quickly as business needs change. It lets teams experiment, test and deliver faster because they're no longer limited by hardware procurement times.
why: Disaster recovery is about restoring service after a major outage.
Capital expenditure is upfront hardware spending, which is what the team avoided.
Fault tolerance is about continuing to run when components fail.
questions.tip: 'Quickly create and tear down' = agility.

questions.q: Which description of the Azure free account is accurate?
opts: It includes free amounts of popular services for 12 months, a credit to use in the first 30 days, and some services that are always free
It gives unlimited use of every Azure service at no cost for one year
It provides a physical server shipped to the customer for testing
It's only available to companies that sign a three-year agreement
questions.e: The Azure free account lets new customers explore Azure. It combines a credit to spend in the first 30 days, 12 months of free amounts of selected popular services, and a set of services that stay free within limits. Usage above the free limits is billed only if you upgrade to pay-as-you-go. Offer details can change, so check the official page.
why: Free amounts are limited per service. They aren't unlimited use of everything.
Azure is delivered from Microsoft's datacenters. No hardware is shipped to customers.
The free account needs no long-term agreement.
questions.tip: Free account = credit for 30 days, 12 months of popular services, and always-free services.

questions.q: Which tool provides a web-based, graphical interface for creating and managing Azure resources?
opts: ARM templates
Azure CLI
Azure PowerShell
The Azure portal
questions.e: The Azure portal is a browser-based console where you can build, manage and monitor everything from simple web apps to complex deployments using a graphical interface. It also offers customisable dashboards and access to Azure Cloud Shell.
why: ARM templates are JSON files that describe resources for declarative deployment, not an interactive interface.
Azure CLI is a command-line tool, not a graphical web interface.
Azure PowerShell is a set of command-line cmdlets for scripting.
questions.tip: Graphical and in the browser = Azure portal.

questions.on: Describe Azure Cloud Shell, Azure CLI, and Azure PowerShell
questions.q: An administrator wants to run Azure commands from a web browser on a borrowed computer without installing any tools. Which option fits best?
opts: Remote Desktop to an on-premises server
Azure Data Box
Azure Cloud Shell
Installing Azure PowerShell locally
questions.e: Azure Cloud Shell is an interactive, authenticated, browser-based shell for managing Azure resources. You choose Bash or PowerShell, and common tools, including Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell, come preinstalled. It opens from the portal or shell.azure.com, so nothing has to be installed locally.
why: Remote Desktop to an on-premises server needs that server and its tools, and doesn't provide a ready Azure shell.
Azure Data Box is a physical device for moving data into Azure, not a command shell.
Installing tools locally contradicts the requirement not to install anything.
questions.tip: 'Browser' plus 'no installation' plus 'commands' = Cloud Shell.

questions.on: Describe Azure Cloud Shell, Azure CLI, and Azure PowerShell
questions.q: An engineer writes Bash scripts that run commands such as 'az vm create' on Linux, macOS and Windows. Which Azure tool is the engineer using?
opts: Azure PowerShell
Azure Advisor
The Azure portal
Azure CLI
questions.e: Azure CLI is a cross-platform command-line tool whose commands start with 'az'. It's popular in Bash scripts and runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, as well as in Azure Cloud Shell. It's ideal for automating repeatable tasks.
why: Azure PowerShell uses cmdlets with verb-noun names such as New-AzVM, not 'az' commands.
Azure Advisor gives recommendations. It doesn't run commands.
The Azure portal is a graphical interface, not a scripting tool.
questions.tip: Commands beginning with 'az' = Azure CLI. Verb-noun such as New-AzVM = Azure PowerShell.

questions.on: Describe Azure regions, region pairs, and sovereign regions
questions.q: What is an Azure region?
opts: A geographical area on the planet containing at least one, and potentially several, datacenters connected by a low-latency network
A logical folder for grouping related resources
A single server rack that hosts one customer's resources
A billing agreement between a customer and Microsoft
questions.e: An Azure region is a geographic area with one or more nearby datacenters linked by a low-latency network. When you deploy most resources, you choose a region, which affects latency to users, data residency and service availability.
why: A logical folder for resources is a resource group.
A rack is far smaller than a region, and racks are shared by many customers.
A billing agreement is associated with a subscription, not a region.
questions.tip: Region = geography plus datacenters.

questions.on: Describe Azure regions, region pairs, and sovereign regions
questions.q: A company's web app is hosted in an Azure region in Western Europe. Users in Australia complain that pages load slowly, although the app performs well for European users. What's the most effective change?
opts: Increase the size of the VMs in the Western Europe region
Purchase reservations for the existing VMs
Deploy an instance of the app in an Azure region in or near Australia
Change the storage redundancy option for the app's data
questions.e: Network latency grows with physical distance. Because European users are fine, the problem is distance, not capacity. Deploying the app in a region close to Australian users (often with traffic routing that sends users to the nearest instance) reduces round-trip time.
why: Bigger VMs add capacity, but the issue is distance-based latency, which VM size doesn't fix.
Reservations change price, not performance.
Storage redundancy affects durability and availability of data, not network latency to distant users.
questions.tip: Slow only for far-away users means latency. Fix it by moving closer.

questions.on: Describe Azure regions, region pairs, and sovereign regions
questions.q: A United States federal agency needs an Azure environment that is physically and logically isolated from the global public Azure regions and operated by screened personnel to meet government requirements. What should it use?
opts: Azure Government
A standard public Azure region in the United States
A region pair between two US regions
An availability zone in a US region
questions.e: Sovereign regions are instances of Azure isolated from the main public cloud. Azure Government serves US government agencies and their partners: its datacenters are physically and logically isolated and operated by screened personnel. Another example is Azure operated by 21Vianet in China.
why: A standard public region shares the global public Azure environment and isn't isolated for government use.
A region pair provides disaster-recovery pairing within public Azure. It doesn't create isolation.
An availability zone is a group of datacenters within a public region. It doesn't create a sovereign environment.
questions.tip: US government isolation = Azure Government (a sovereign region).

questions.q: Which statement best describes an Azure availability zone?
opts: A sovereign instance of Azure for governments
A physically separate location within an Azure region, made up of one or more datacenters with independent power, cooling and networking
A logical group of virtual machines on the same host
A separate Azure region at least 300 miles away
questions.e: Availability zones are physically separate groups of datacenters within one region, each with independent power, cooling and networking, connected by high-speed private links. Deploying across zones protects applications from a datacenter-level failure. Not every region supports zones.
why: Sovereign regions are isolated Azure instances, not zones.
Zones span datacenters. They aren't groups of VMs on one host.
A separate region is a different concept. Zones are inside one region.
questions.tip: Zone = separate datacenter(s) inside one region.

questions.q: Azure SQL Database and Azure Cosmos DB belong to which category of cloud service?
opts: Databases
Networking
Monitoring
Identity
questions.e: Both are managed database services. Azure SQL Database is a relational database service built on SQL Server. Azure Cosmos DB is a globally distributed NoSQL database. Because they're managed, Microsoft handles much of the patching, backups and availability.
why: Networking services connect resources, for example Azure Virtual Network.
Monitoring services collect and analyse telemetry, for example Azure Monitor.
Identity services manage users and sign-in, for example Microsoft Entra ID.
questions.tip: Names containing 'SQL' or 'DB' point to databases.

questions.on: Describe directory services: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft Entra Domain Services
questions.q: An older training document refers to 'Azure Active Directory (Azure AD)'. What is the current name of this Microsoft cloud identity service?
opts: Microsoft Defender for Cloud
Microsoft Entra ID
Microsoft Purview
Azure Policy
questions.e: Microsoft renamed Azure Active Directory to Microsoft Entra ID in 2023. It's Microsoft's cloud-based identity and access management service, handling users, groups, sign-in, multifactor authentication and single sign-on. The current exam uses the Entra name, so treat 'Azure AD' as outdated terminology.
why: Microsoft Defender for Cloud is a security posture and threat-protection service, not the identity directory.
Microsoft Purview handles data governance, risk and compliance.
Azure Policy enforces governance rules on resources.
questions.tip: Azure AD has been renamed Microsoft Entra ID.

questions.q: A physical disk fails in an Azure datacenter on a server that stores data for a company's storage account. Who is responsible for replacing the failed disk?
opts: Microsoft
The company that owns the storage account
The company's internet service provider
The company and Microsoft jointly, through a support ticket the company must open
questions.e: Physical hardware in Azure datacenters is always Microsoft's responsibility. Azure Storage also keeps multiple copies of data, so a single disk failure doesn't cause data loss. Microsoft detects and replaces failed hardware without any customer action.
why: Customers have no access to physical hardware and aren't responsible for it.
An ISP provides connectivity, not datacenter maintenance.
No customer ticket is needed. Hardware replacement happens automatically on Microsoft's side.
questions.tip: Failed physical hardware is always the provider's job.

questions.on: Identify appropriate use cases for each cloud service type
questions.q: A startup has three requirements for its new web application: no upfront hardware spending, the ability to handle unpredictable traffic spikes automatically, and no responsibility for patching operating systems. Which approach meets all three?
opts: On-premises servers bought with extra spare capacity
IaaS virtual machines in a public cloud, sized for the expected peak
A private cloud built in the startup's own datacenter
A PaaS web hosting service in a public cloud, with autoscaling enabled
questions.e: Public cloud removes upfront hardware spending. A PaaS hosting service such as Azure App Service manages the operating system, which removes the patching responsibility. Autoscaling adjusts instance count to demand automatically. Only this combination satisfies all three requirements.
why: Buying servers is upfront spending, and the startup would patch everything.
IaaS VMs avoid hardware spending, but the startup would patch the OS, and fixed peak sizing doesn't adapt automatically.
A private cloud needs hardware investment and operating system management by the startup.
questions.tip: Check every requirement against every option. Only one usually satisfies all of them.

questions.on: Describe virtual networking: VNets, subnets, peering, Azure DNS, VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute
questions.q: Which of these is a networking service in Azure?
opts: Azure Functions
Azure Virtual Network
Azure Cosmos DB
Azure Blob Storage
questions.e: Azure Virtual Network (VNet) lets Azure resources communicate with each other, with the internet and with on-premises networks in a private, isolated network space. It's the foundation of networking in Azure.
why: Azure Functions is a serverless compute service.
Azure Cosmos DB is a NoSQL database service.
Azure Blob Storage is an object storage service.
questions.tip: 'Network' in the name and connecting resources = networking.

questions.q: Cloud computing is often compared to an electricity utility. Which part of the comparison is most accurate?
opts: Only one customer at a time can draw from the supply
You must build your own power station before you can use it
You consume capacity when you need it and pay for what you use, without owning the infrastructure that produces it
You pay the same flat amount however much you use
questions.e: Like electricity from the grid, cloud resources are produced at large scale by a provider, delivered on demand, metered and billed by consumption. You don't need to own the 'power plant' (the datacenter) to benefit from it.
why: Utilities and clouds serve many customers at once. That's resource pooling.
Building your own power station is like owning a datacenter, which cloud avoids.
Utility and cloud billing are metered, not a flat amount however much you use.
questions.tip: Utility analogy = on demand, metered, provider owns the plant.

questions.on: Describe Azure regions, region pairs, and sovereign regions
questions.q: A company is legally required to store customer data within its own country. It wants to use Azure. What is the most appropriate first step?
opts: Deploy the data-storing resources in an Azure region located in that country, and confirm how each service handles data location
Use a content delivery network so data stays near users
Select an availability zone, because zones guarantee the country where data is stored
Use a private cloud, because public clouds can't keep data in one country
questions.e: With Azure you choose the region where most resources and their data live, which helps meet data-residency requirements. Some services are global or may replicate data elsewhere (for example, certain redundancy options copy data to a paired region), so you also confirm each service's data-location behaviour.
why: A CDN caches copies of content at many edge locations, which can work against keeping data in one country.
Zones exist inside a region. Choosing the region determines the geography, and zones alone don't decide it.
Public clouds let you pick regions, so a private cloud isn't the only way to meet residency rules.
questions.tip: Data residency usually starts with region selection.

questions.on: Identify appropriate use cases for each cloud model
questions.q: A company runs its order-processing system on-premises for normal workloads. During quarterly peaks, it automatically runs extra processing capacity in Azure, then releases it afterwards. Which cloud model enables this?
opts: Software as a service
Public cloud only
Hybrid cloud
Private cloud
questions.e: Using public cloud capacity to handle overflow from on-premises infrastructure is often called cloud bursting, and it's a common hybrid cloud use case. The company keeps its existing investment for steady demand and pays for public cloud resources only while the peaks last.
why: SaaS is a service type, not a deployment model, and the company runs its own system.
The baseline still runs on-premises, so it isn't public cloud only.
A private cloud alone can't burst into public cloud capacity.
questions.tip: On-premises baseline plus cloud for peaks = hybrid (cloud bursting).

questions.q: In cloud terminology, what does 'provisioning' a resource mean?
opts: Allocating and configuring the resource so it's ready to use
Moving the resource to another provider
Creating an invoice for the resource
Permanently deleting the resource
questions.e: Provisioning is the process of creating and setting up a resource, such as a VM, a database or a storage account, so it's available for use. In the cloud this is usually self-service and takes minutes, through the portal, CLI, APIs or templates.
why: Moving between providers is migration.
Invoicing is a billing activity, not provisioning.
Deleting a resource is deprovisioning, the opposite.
questions.tip: Provision = create and set up.

questions.on: Identify appropriate use cases for each cloud service type
questions.q: A company plans to move its existing virtual machines to Azure with as few changes as possible, keeping the same operating systems and applications. Which service type is typically used for this 'lift and shift' migration?
opts: Platform as a service (PaaS)
Infrastructure as a service (IaaS)
Serverless computing
Software as a service (SaaS)
questions.e: Lift and shift means moving workloads to the cloud as-is, without redesigning them. IaaS virtual machines let you run the same operating systems and applications you used on-premises, which makes IaaS the natural target. Tools such as Azure Migrate help with assessment and migration.
why: PaaS usually needs some application changes, so it isn't 'as few changes as possible'.
Serverless needs the code to be restructured into event-driven functions.
SaaS replaces your app with the provider's finished software. It doesn't move your existing VMs.
questions.tip: 'As-is', 'minimal change' and 'existing VMs' = IaaS.

questions.q: A finance director says: 'Once we move to the cloud, our IT costs will always go down.' Which response is most accurate?
opts: That's correct, because cloud resources are free after migration
That's incorrect, because cloud always costs more than on-premises
That's correct, because cloud prices are fixed regardless of usage
Costs can go down, but they depend on how resources are used and managed. Oversized or idle resources keep generating charges
questions.e: The cloud removes upfront hardware costs and lets you pay for what you use, but that cuts both ways: resources left running, oversized VMs or unnecessary data transfer all cost money. Savings come from right-sizing, shutting down idle resources, using commitment discounts where appropriate, and monitoring costs with tools such as Microsoft Cost Management.
why: Cloud resources aren't free. They're billed by consumption.
Cloud isn't always more expensive. Costs depend on workload and management.
Consumption pricing varies with usage. It isn't fixed.
questions.tip: Be wary of 'always' answers about cost. Cloud costs follow usage.

questions.q: In cloud computing, what does the term 'workload' usually refer to?
opts: The number of employees in the IT department
A physical server delivered by the provider
An application or set of resources that together deliver a business capability
The monthly invoice from the provider
questions.e: A workload is a collection of application resources, such as VMs, databases, storage and networking, that supports a business process or capability, for example an e-commerce site or a payroll system. Cloud planning and migration are usually discussed workload by workload.
why: IT staffing levels aren't workloads.
Providers don't deliver physical servers to customers.
An invoice is a billing document, not a workload.
questions.tip: Workload = the app and its resources.

questions.on: Describe the benefits of reliability and predictability in the cloud
questions.q: A company has only one datacenter and no secondary site for disaster recovery. Building a second datacenter would be too expensive. How can the cloud help?
opts: Replicate critical workloads to Azure and fail over to them if the primary datacenter fails, paying mainly for storage and replication until a failover happens
Rely on the internet service provider to restore the servers after a disaster
Buy a second set of servers and ship them to Microsoft for storage
Increase the size of the servers in the existing datacenter
questions.e: The cloud can act as a disaster-recovery site without the cost of a second physical datacenter. Workloads are replicated to Azure (for example with Azure Site Recovery), and in a disaster they're started in Azure. Because compute is consumption-based, most costs before failover are for storage and replication.
why: An ISP doesn't restore servers or data.
Microsoft doesn't store customer-owned servers. Azure provides the infrastructure itself.
Larger servers in the same datacenter still fail together in a disaster.
questions.tip: No second site? Use the cloud as the second site.

questions.q:
Evaluate these statements about serverless computing.
1. On a consumption plan, you're typically billed based on executions and the resources used while code runs.
2. You must install operating system patches on the servers that run your code.
3. The platform automatically scales to respond to the number of incoming events.
Which statements are true?
opts: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
questions.e: Serverless platforms such as Azure Functions on a consumption plan bill per execution and the resources used during execution (statement 1 is true), and scale automatically with event load (statement 3 is true). The provider manages the servers and operating system, so statement 2 is false.
why: Statement 2 is false, and true statement 1 is left out.
Statement 2 is the only false statement here.
Statement 2 is false. Serverless removes OS patching from you.
questions.tip: Serverless = pay per execution, auto-scale, no server management.

questions.q: Which Azure service is an example of serverless compute?
opts: Azure Virtual Desktop
Azure Virtual Machines
Azure Dedicated Host
Azure Functions
questions.e: Azure Functions is an event-driven, serverless compute service. You write small pieces of code (functions) that run in response to triggers such as HTTP requests, timers, queue messages or file uploads. On the Consumption or Flex Consumption plans it scales automatically, and you pay mainly for what runs.
why: Azure Virtual Desktop delivers virtual desktops to users. It isn't event-driven code hosting.
Virtual machines are IaaS. You manage the OS and pay while they run.
Dedicated Host provides whole physical servers, which is the opposite of serverless.
questions.tip: Functions = serverless code. Logic Apps = serverless workflows.

questions.on: Describe Azure regions, region pairs, and sovereign regions
questions.q: A European company wants to launch its service for customers in Southeast Asia within a week, but doesn't have any datacenter there. What does Azure allow it to do?
opts: Wait until Microsoft builds a dedicated region for the company
Order hardware for Microsoft to install in a new Asian datacenter for the company
Deploy its application to an existing Azure region in Southeast Asia within minutes or hours
