Serve Asian customers only from Europe, because cloud regions can't be changed
questions.e: Azure has regions across the world. Customers can deploy resources to any available region on demand, which gives global reach without building or leasing datacenters. That makes quick international expansion practical.
why: Existing regions are shared by many customers. No dedicated region is needed.
Customers don't order hardware for Microsoft datacenters. Capacity is already available to rent.
You can deploy to any available region. You're not locked to one.
questions.tip: Global expansion without building datacenters is a core cloud benefit.

questions.q: Is the following statement true or false? 'When you create a virtual machine in Azure, you can choose which specific physical host server in the datacenter it runs on.'
opts: True. Every VM is pinned to a host chosen by the customer
False. VMs in Azure don't run on physical hardware
True, but only when using the Azure portal
False. You choose a region (and optionally an availability zone or VM size), and Azure places the VM on suitable hardware
questions.e: Cloud computing abstracts the physical layer. You specify the region, VM size, image and optionally an availability zone, and Azure decides which physical host to use. (Azure Dedicated Host is a special option that gives you a whole physical server, but you still don't pick racks or buildings.)
why: Customers don't pick individual hosts in normal Azure deployments.
VMs always run on physical hardware. The abstraction hides it; it doesn't remove it.
The portal, CLI and templates all work the same way. None of them lets you pick a host.
questions.tip: Cloud abstracts hardware. You choose where geographically, not which box.

questions.q: Which statement about capacity planning in the cloud is most accurate?
opts: Capacity can only be changed once a year during contract renewal
You still plan capacity, but you can adjust it quickly as demand changes instead of committing to hardware for years
Capacity planning is no longer needed, because cloud resources are unlimited and free
You must buy all the capacity you'll need for the next five years when you sign up
questions.e: Cloud doesn't remove the need to think about capacity, but it lowers the cost of getting it wrong. You can start with a reasonable estimate and then scale up, out, down or in within minutes, rather than guessing years ahead and buying hardware to match.
why: Capacity can be changed at any time, not just at renewal.
Cloud capacity is large but neither unlimited nor free. Every resource is billed.
Nothing needs to be bought up front. That's the on-premises model.
questions.tip: The cloud makes capacity decisions reversible and quick. It doesn't make them unnecessary.

questions.q: A company compares running 20 on-premises servers with running equivalent Azure virtual machines. Which cost does the company no longer pay directly after moving to Azure VMs?
opts: Protecting its business data and user accounts
Training staff to use and manage its applications
Licensing and patching its own application software
Purchasing server hardware and paying for datacenter power and cooling
questions.e: With IaaS VMs, Microsoft buys and runs the hardware, power, cooling and physical facilities, and these costs are built into the VM's usage price. The customer still pays for and manages its own applications, licences it brings, staff skills, and the protection of its data and identities.
why: Data and account protection are always the customer's responsibility.
Staff still need skills to run applications, so training costs don't disappear.
Application software, its licences and its patching remain the customer's concern in IaaS.
questions.tip: In IaaS the physical costs vanish from your books, but everything above the hypervisor remains yours.

questions.on: Describe the benefits of high availability and scalability in the cloud
questions.q: A service has a service-level agreement (SLA) promising 99.9% uptime per month. Approximately how much downtime does this allow in a 30-day month?
opts: About 4 minutes
About 43 minutes
About 1 day
About 7 hours
questions.e: A 30-day month has 43,200 minutes. 99.9% uptime allows 0.1% downtime: 43,200 × 0.001 ≈ 43 minutes. Each extra 'nine' cuts allowed downtime by about ten times. 99.99% allows about 4.3 minutes per month, and 99% allows about 7.2 hours.
why: About 4 minutes matches 99.99% uptime, not 99.9%.
About a day would be roughly 96.7% uptime, far below 99.9%.
About 7 hours matches 99% uptime.
questions.tip: 99.9% ≈ 43 minutes a month. 99.99% ≈ 4 minutes. 99% ≈ 7 hours.

questions.on: Describe the benefits of high availability and scalability in the cloud
questions.q: What is the key difference between high availability and fault tolerance?
opts: Fault tolerance is cheaper because it needs fewer resources
High availability applies only to storage, while fault tolerance applies only to compute
They are two names for the same concept
High availability aims to minimise downtime, while fault tolerance aims for no interruption at all when a component fails, through full redundancy
questions.e: High availability designs keep downtime low and recover quickly, accepting that brief interruptions may happen, and are usually measured as an SLA percentage. Fault tolerance goes further: redundant components take over instantly so users notice no interruption. Fault tolerance generally costs more because it needs duplicate resources running at all times.
why: Fault tolerance usually costs more, because of fully redundant, always-on components.
Both concepts apply to any layer: compute, storage and networking.
They're related but not identical. Fault tolerance is a stricter goal.
questions.tip: HA = minimal downtime. Fault tolerance = zero interruption from a failure.

questions.on: Describe Azure regions, region pairs, and sovereign regions
questions.q: What does network latency measure?
opts: The number of virtual machines in a subscription
The percentage of time a service is available
The time it takes for data to travel between a client and a server
The amount of data stored in a database
questions.e: Latency is the delay in communication, usually measured in milliseconds of round-trip time. It increases with physical distance and network hops, which is why choosing a region close to users improves responsiveness.
why: VM count is an inventory figure, not a network measurement.
Percentage of time available is availability (uptime).
Data volume is a storage measurement, not a measure of delay.
questions.tip: Latency = delay, which grows with distance.

questions.on: Describe factors that can affect costs in Azure
questions.q: A company moves large amounts of data both into and out of Azure every month. Which statement about Azure data transfer charges is generally correct?
opts: Inbound data transfer is charged, but outbound is always free
Data transfer is billed only when it happens inside an availability zone
Both inbound and outbound data transfer are always free
Data transferred into Azure is free, while data transferred out of Azure regions to the internet is generally charged beyond a free monthly allowance
questions.e: Azure doesn't charge for inbound data transfer (ingress). Outbound transfer (egress) from Azure regions to the internet is billed per gigabyte after a free monthly allowance. Rates vary by source region, and some traffic between regions or zones can also be charged. Check the official bandwidth pricing page for current details.
why: This reverses the model. Inbound is the free direction.
Charges depend on direction and route, not just on movement inside a zone.
Outbound data transfer is generally billed, so it isn't all free.
questions.tip: Data in is free. Data out costs money. Egress is a common hidden cost factor.

questions.on: Describe the benefits of high availability and scalability in the cloud
questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes elasticity from scalability?
opts: Elasticity is the ability to scale automatically, up or down, in response to changing demand
Elasticity applies only to adding storage, never compute
Elasticity means a system never needs more resources
Elasticity requires buying new hardware for each change
questions.e: Scalability is the ability to increase or decrease resources to handle load, whether manually or automatically. Elasticity is the automatic form: the system adds resources when demand rises and removes them when it falls, often through autoscale rules, so you only pay for the capacity you need at each moment.
why: Elasticity applies to compute, storage and other resources.
Elastic systems do need more resources under load. They obtain them automatically.
Elasticity in the cloud uses the provider's pooled capacity, so no hardware purchase is involved.
questions.tip: Elastic = automatic scaling in both directions.

questions.on: Describe Azure regions, region pairs, and sovereign regions
questions.q: Which is a benefit of Azure region pairs?
opts: All data is automatically copied to the paired region for every service at no cost
Region pairs let customers choose the physical server for each VM
Both regions in a pair are always in the same physical building
Planned platform updates are rolled out to one region of a pair at a time, and recovery of one region per pair is prioritised during a broad outage
questions.e: Many Azure regions are paired with another region in the same geography, usually far apart (often at least 300 miles) to reduce the chance of both being affected at once. Microsoft rolls out updates to one region in a pair at a time and prioritises restoring one region per pair in a widespread outage. Some services, such as geo-redundant storage, replicate to the paired region. Newer regions may have no pair and rely on availability zones instead.
why: Cross-region replication isn't automatic for every service. It depends on the service and configuration, and may cost extra.
Region pairs don't give control over physical servers.
Paired regions are deliberately separated by large distances, not in the same building.
questions.tip: Region pairs = staggered updates, prioritised recovery, and an optional replication target.

questions.q: A team wants every test environment to be created identically and repeatably, with the definition stored in version control. Which approach supports this?
opts: Buying identical physical servers for every environment
Infrastructure as code, such as ARM templates or Bicep files
Clicking through the Azure portal manually each time
Writing instructions in a document for each administrator to follow
questions.e: Infrastructure as code (IaC) describes resources in files that tools such as Azure Resource Manager deploy. Because the definition is code, it can be versioned, reviewed and redeployed consistently, which removes the drift that manual steps cause. ARM templates (JSON) and Bicep are Azure's native IaC languages.
why: Physical servers are the opposite of fast, repeatable cloud environments.
Manual portal work is error-prone and not reliably repeatable.
Written instructions depend on people following them exactly, which isn't consistent.
questions.tip: 'Repeatable' and 'version control' = infrastructure as code.

questions.on: Describe Azure resources and resource groups
questions.q: What is an Azure resource group?
opts: A pricing tier for virtual machines
A group of users who share the same password
A logical container that holds related Azure resources so they can be managed together
A physical datacenter that stores a company's resources
questions.e: A resource group is a logical container for resources such as VMs, storage accounts and databases that share a lifecycle. You can apply access control, policies and tags at the resource group level, and deleting a resource group deletes everything in it. Every resource belongs to exactly one resource group.
why: Pricing tiers are VM sizes or SKUs, not resource groups.
Groups of users are managed in Microsoft Entra ID, and users don't share passwords.
Resource groups are logical, not physical.
questions.tip: Resource group = logical folder for resources.

questions.q: A company wants each department to pay for exactly the cloud resources it uses, instead of splitting IT costs equally. Which cloud characteristic makes this practical?
opts: Measured, consumption-based billing that records usage per resource
Hardware ownership by the company
Broad network access from any device
Multitenancy at the physical host level
questions.e: Because cloud usage is metered per resource, costs can be traced to the resources each department runs. With tools such as tags and Microsoft Cost Management, organisations can report and charge back costs to departments, projects or cost centres.
why: The company doesn't own the hardware in the cloud. Metering is what enables allocation.
Device access doesn't help attribute costs.
Multitenancy is about the provider sharing hardware among customers, not internal cost allocation.
questions.tip: 'Charge departments for what they use' relies on metering, with tags to group costs.

questions.on: Identify appropriate use cases for each cloud model
questions.q: Compared with a public cloud, what is a main disadvantage of a private cloud hosted in the company's own datacenter?
opts: The company has less control over security configuration
Other organisations share the same hardware
The company can't use virtualization
The company must buy, maintain and upgrade the hardware, which needs capital spending and in-house expertise
questions.e: A private cloud gives maximum control, but the organisation carries the full cost of purchasing hardware, running the facility, and maintaining and updating everything. It also loses the near-unlimited scale and global reach of a public cloud.
why: Private clouds give more control over security, not less.
Hardware sharing among organisations describes a public cloud.
Private clouds are built on virtualization.
questions.tip: Private cloud trade-off: more control, but you pay for and run everything.

questions.on: Define cloud models, including public, private, and hybrid
questions.q: Which list contains only cloud deployment models?
opts: CapEx, OpEx, consumption
Public, private, hybrid
Compute, storage, networking
IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
questions.e: Deployment models describe where the cloud runs and who uses it: public, private, hybrid (and multicloud). Service types (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) describe how much the provider manages. Compute, storage and networking are resource categories, and CapEx and OpEx are spending types.
why: CapEx, OpEx and consumption describe spending, not deployment.
Compute, storage and networking are resource categories.
IaaS, PaaS and SaaS are service types, not deployment models.
questions.tip: Deployment model = where it runs. Service type = how much is managed for you.

questions.on: Identify appropriate use cases for each cloud model
questions.q: A defence contractor already owns a modern datacenter, has steady and predictable demand, and is contractually required to keep complete control over the physical hardware that runs a classified workload. Which cloud model fits that workload best?
opts: Multicloud across two public providers
Public cloud
Private cloud
Software as a service
questions.e: A private cloud gives an organisation exclusive use of the infrastructure and full control over hardware and security. With an existing datacenter, predictable demand and a contractual need for physical control, the main public cloud advantages (no CapEx, elastic scale) matter less than control.
why: Using two public providers still means no control of physical hardware.
Public cloud hardware is owned and controlled by the provider, which breaks the contractual requirement.
SaaS is a service type in which the provider controls everything below the application.
questions.tip: 'Must control the physical hardware' points to private cloud.

questions.on: Compare compute types, including containers, virtual machines, and functions
questions.q: How do containers differ from virtual machines?
opts: Containers replace the need for any compute resources
Containers package an application with its dependencies and share the host operating system kernel, so they're lighter and start faster than VMs
Containers can only run in on-premises datacenters
Containers each include a full guest operating system, so they're heavier than VMs
questions.e: A VM virtualizes hardware and runs a full guest OS. A container virtualizes the operating system: it bundles the app and its libraries but shares the host's kernel. Containers are small, start in seconds and are portable across environments. Azure runs them through services such as Azure Container Instances, Azure Container Apps and Azure Kubernetes Service.
why: Containers still need compute resources to run on.
Containers run in the cloud and on-premises alike. Portability is one of their strengths.
This describes VMs. Containers don't include a full guest OS.
questions.tip: VM = virtualized hardware with a full OS. Container = virtualized OS, lightweight.

questions.q: A company runs SQL Server on its own VMs and spends a lot of time on patching, backups and high-availability configuration. Which option most reduces this effort while keeping a relational SQL database?
opts: Move SQL Server to larger Azure VMs
Keep SQL Server on-premises and add more administrators
Move to Azure SQL Database, a PaaS service where Microsoft handles patching, backups and built-in high availability
Move the data into Azure Blob Storage
questions.e: Azure SQL Database is a fully managed relational database (PaaS). Microsoft manages the operating system and database engine patching, automated backups and built-in high availability, so the team can focus on schema, queries and data instead.
why: SQL Server on VMs is IaaS. The company would still patch and back it up.
Adding administrators increases cost and doesn't reduce the work itself.
Blob Storage holds unstructured objects. It isn't a relational SQL database.
questions.tip: 'Managed', with patching and backups handled for you = PaaS.

questions.q: As a workload moves from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS, how does the customer's share of management responsibility change?
opts: It decreases, because the provider manages more of the stack at each step
It stays exactly the same in all three service types
It drops to zero in SaaS, including for data and accounts
It increases, because the customer manages more of the stack at each step
questions.e: In IaaS the customer manages the OS, middleware, applications and data. PaaS shifts the OS and runtime to the provider. SaaS shifts the application too. Data, devices, and accounts and identities always remain the customer's responsibility, even in SaaS.
why: Responsibilities shift significantly between the service types.
Even in SaaS the customer keeps responsibility for data, devices and identities.
This reverses the direction. The customer does less at each step.
questions.tip: IaaS → PaaS → SaaS: less for you each step, but never nothing.

questions.q: Is the following statement true or false? 'Azure customers can visit the datacenters that host their resources to inspect their servers.'
opts: False. Azure doesn't use physical datacenters
True, but only for customers using IaaS
False. Azure datacenters aren't directly accessible to customers, and Microsoft strictly controls physical access
True. Customers can visit by booking a slot in the Azure portal
questions.e: Microsoft tightly controls physical access to Azure datacenters as part of its responsibility for physical security. Customers interact with Azure only through the portal, tools and APIs. They choose regions, not buildings, and never handle the hardware.
why: Azure runs on physical datacenters. Customers just can't access them.
IaaS doesn't grant physical access. The physical layer is always Microsoft's.
No portal feature books datacenter visits.
questions.tip: Physical access = Microsoft only.

questions.q: When comparing on-premises infrastructure with the cloud, why should a company consider total cost of ownership (TCO) rather than only the purchase price of servers?
opts: TCO ignores staffing costs because they don't change
TCO counts only the monthly cloud bill
TCO applies only to software licences
TCO includes hidden ongoing costs such as power, cooling, facilities, maintenance, staff time and hardware refreshes
questions.e: The server price is only part of the cost of on-premises IT. Electricity, cooling, floor space, network equipment, maintenance contracts, administrator time, and the replacement of hardware every few years all add up. A fair comparison with cloud pricing has to include them.
why: Staff time is often one of the largest parts of TCO.
TCO covers all costs, on-premises and cloud, not just one bill.
Licences are one item among many in TCO.
questions.tip: TCO = everything it costs to own and run, not just the purchase price.

questions.q: From an accounting perspective, how does cloud spending (OpEx) typically differ from buying servers (CapEx)?
opts: Neither can ever be deducted from taxable income
CapEx is deducted immediately, while OpEx must be depreciated over several years
OpEx can usually be deducted in the same year it's incurred, while CapEx is depreciated over the asset's useful life
OpEx and CapEx are recorded identically in all cases
questions.e: Capital expenditure buys assets whose cost is spread over several years through depreciation. Operational expenditure is generally deducted in the year it's spent. This is one reason organisations value the cloud's OpEx model: it avoids large upfront investments and matches spending to use. Exact rules vary by country.
why: Both are generally deductible, just on different timelines.
This reverses the usual treatment. CapEx is the one that is depreciated.
They're treated differently, and that difference is part of the cloud's financial appeal.
questions.tip: CapEx = depreciated over years. OpEx = deducted in the year spent.

questions.q: A team's Azure bill doubles one month. Investigation shows that a set of large development VMs were left running over several weekends when nobody was using them. Which statement best explains the cause and the fix?
opts: The bill doubled because Azure prices change every weekend
Azure charged a penalty for weekend usage; contact support to remove it
The VMs must be converted to Spot VMs, because pay-as-you-go VMs can't be stopped
Under consumption-based billing, running VMs cost money even when idle; schedule them to stop and deallocate when not needed
questions.e: With consumption pricing you pay for compute while a VM is allocated, whether or not anyone uses it. Stopping and deallocating idle VMs (for example with auto-shutdown schedules) stops compute charges. Attached disks still incur storage charges. Monitoring with Cost Management budgets and alerts helps catch this early.
why: Azure prices don't change on weekends.
Azure doesn't apply weekend penalties. The VMs were simply billed for running.
Pay-as-you-go VMs can be stopped and deallocated at any time.
questions.tip: Idle but running still costs money. Stop and deallocate to save.

questions.q: A test environment is used only between 09:00 and 17:00 on weekdays. Which change takes best advantage of the consumption-based model to reduce cost?
opts: Increase the VM sizes so tests run faster
Move the test VMs to a private cloud
Automatically stop and deallocate the test VMs outside working hours
Buy three-year reservations for the test VMs
questions.e: Because compute is billed while VMs run, shutting them down during the roughly 75% of the week when nobody uses them cuts compute charges substantially. Azure VMs support auto-shutdown schedules, and automation can start them again each morning.
why: Larger VMs cost more per hour and don't address idle time.
A private cloud requires buying hardware, which defeats the purpose of saving money.
Reservations are best for VMs that run continuously. Paying a commitment for machines idle most of the week wastes money.
questions.tip: Part-time workloads: pay-as-you-go plus scheduled shutdown.

questions.q: A five-person company wants enterprise-grade infrastructure, such as global datacenters and built-in redundancy, but has no IT budget for hardware. How does the cloud help?
opts: It requires the company to buy a minimum number of servers
It's only available to companies with more than 1,000 employees
It requires the company to build its own datacenter first
It gives access to large-scale infrastructure on a pay-as-you-go basis, without upfront investment
questions.e: Cloud computing levels the playing field. A small business can use the same global, redundant infrastructure that large enterprises use, paying only for what it consumes and starting small with no capital spending.
why: No server purchase is needed. Resources are rented.
Azure is available to organisations and individuals of any size.
No datacenter is needed. That's the point of using the cloud.
questions.tip: Cloud = enterprise-scale capability without enterprise-scale upfront cost.

questions.on: Identify appropriate use cases for each cloud model
questions.q: Which requirement can't be met by using a public cloud alone?
opts: The company needs to scale quickly for seasonal demand
The company wants to avoid upfront hardware costs
Company policy requires all servers to be located in buildings that the company itself owns and physically controls
The company wants to deploy applications in several countries
questions.e: Public cloud infrastructure lives in the provider's datacenters, which the provider owns and controls. A policy requiring company-owned, company-controlled buildings needs a private cloud or on-premises infrastructure (possibly as part of a hybrid design). The other requirements are classic public cloud strengths.
why: Rapid seasonal scaling is a core public cloud benefit.
Avoiding upfront hardware costs is a core public cloud benefit.
Multi-country deployment is easy with Azure's global regions.
questions.tip: In 'cannot be met' questions, look for the requirement about physical ownership.

questions.on: Identify appropriate use cases for each cloud service type
questions.q: Which set correctly matches each cloud service type to an Azure or Microsoft example?
opts: IaaS: Azure Virtual Machines. PaaS: Microsoft 365. SaaS: Azure App Service
IaaS: Microsoft 365. PaaS: Azure Virtual Machines. SaaS: Azure App Service
IaaS: Azure App Service. PaaS: Microsoft 365. SaaS: Azure Virtual Machines
IaaS: Azure Virtual Machines. PaaS: Azure App Service. SaaS: Microsoft 365
questions.e: Azure Virtual Machines are IaaS: you manage the OS and everything above it. Azure App Service is PaaS: you deploy code to a managed platform. Microsoft 365 is SaaS: complete applications that users simply use. Memorising one anchor example for each type helps with many exam questions.
why: The IaaS pairing is right, but Microsoft 365 is SaaS (not PaaS) and App Service is PaaS (not SaaS).
Every pairing in this set is wrong. Microsoft 365 isn't IaaS, VMs aren't PaaS, and App Service isn't SaaS.
Every pairing is wrong. App Service is PaaS, Microsoft 365 is SaaS, and VMs are IaaS.
questions.tip: Anchors: VMs = IaaS, App Service = PaaS, Microsoft 365 = SaaS.
